162.title: My God, why (Psalm 21 [22])
162.hook: the psalm Jesus prayed from the cross, which ends in praise
162.howItsDone: Catholics hear Psalm 21 [22] as the responsorial psalm on Palm Sunday, just before the Passion is read, and pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours; many pray its first line in times of desolation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the firmament, a sky that speaks without words. Your line was the sky is preaching. Today, a psalm from the dark.

Good Friday, the ninth hour. Jesus has been on the cross since morning. The sky has gone dark. Then, the Gospels say, he cries out with a loud voice, in his own language, words bystanders mishear. Matthew writes them down: "Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani? that is, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" For two thousand years, people have stopped at that sentence. It sounds like the bottom of the world. But anyone there who knew the psalms would have recognized it. He wasn't inventing those words. He was praying them.
screen: `THE NINTH HOUR.` → `MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY?` → `HE WAS PRAYING A PSALM.`

segments.voice: They're the first line of Psalm 21 in the Douay, 22 in most Bibles: "O God my God, look upon me: why hast thou forsaken me?" In the ancient world, a psalm was often named by its first line, the way we'd name a song by its opening words. So many readers hear Jesus calling up the whole psalm. Its first half is as dark as scripture gets. The one praying is mocked; people shake their heads and say, let God rescue him, then. He's poured out like water, his bones out of joint, his heart like melting wax, his tongue stuck to his jaw. "They parted my garments amongst them; and upon my vesture they cast lots." The Gospels tell that very thing happening at the foot of the cross, and John quotes the line. Then, near the end, the psalm stops asking why and starts thanking. God has not despised the poor man's cry. The poor will eat and be filled. All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and people not yet born will be told what God has done. It begins in abandonment and ends with the whole world praising. Christians have thought for centuries about how to understand Jesus praying this. The Church holds both at once: he truly felt the full weight of that cry, and he prayed it as a psalm of trust whose ending he knew. Either way, the words were given to anyone who has ever felt forsaken.
screen: `A PSALM NAMED BY ITS FIRST LINE.` · `MOCKED, POURED OUT LIKE WATER.` · `THEY CAST LOTS FOR HIS VESTURE.` · `IT ENDS IN PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who feels abandoned right now, grieving, sick, lonely, far from home or far from God, and without trying to fix it, stand next to them in your mind. If you pray, say the psalm's first line for them, honestly, the way Jesus did: my God, my God, why? If you don't, simply hold them in your attention.
My God. The cry that opens Psalm 21, prayed by Jesus from the cross, from a psalm that begins forsaken and ends in praise. Today's word.
Your line: even this is prayer. A why, said honestly, still counts. See you tomorrow.

163.title: The Lord ruleth me (Psalm 22 [23])
163.hook: green pastures, still waters, and the valley of the shadow
163.howItsDone: Catholics often hear Psalm 22 [23] at funeral Masses and on Good Shepherd Sunday, and pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours; many know it by heart and pray it at bedsides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, my God, the psalm from the cross that ends in praise. Your line was even this is prayer. Today, the next psalm in the book.

A funeral Mass, a hospital bedside, a film where a soldier waits for dawn: this psalm turns up in all of them, and plenty of people who have never opened a Bible can say its first line. The Lord is my shepherd. But open the Douay-Rheims, the Bible English-speaking Catholics used for generations, and it starts with different words. Same psalm, same care, but a different first verb, and it changes the picture.
screen: `AT FUNERALS, AT BEDSIDES.` → `ITS FIRST LINE, BY HEART.` → `THE DOUAY STARTS DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: It's Psalm 22 in the Douay, 23 in most Bibles: "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing." Ruleth, because the Douay follows the Latin, Dominus regit me, the Lord guides me, steers me. The Hebrew says, more simply, the Lord is my shepherd. Both are about the same care: someone who knows the way and leads. Then the famous pictures. "He hath set me in a place of pasture. He hath brought me up, on the water of refreshment." A place to drink and rest. Then the dark part, which the psalm doesn't skip: "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me." The shepherd doesn't lead around the valley. He leads through it. And the grammar changes: until now the psalm talks about God, he, he, he. In the valley it talks to God: thou art with me. Then a table set before enemies, a head anointed with oil, and a cup: "my chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it!" Some early Christians heard the sacraments here. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, connected it with the newly baptized at Easter: the water of refreshment was the font, the oil was the anointing, the table and the chalice were their first Eucharist. It ends with goodness and mercy following all the days of life, and a home in the house of the Lord.
screen: `RULETH: THE LORD GUIDES ME.` · `WATER OF REFRESHMENT.` · `THROUGH THE VALLEY, NOT AROUND.` · `A TABLE, OIL, A CHALICE.`

segments.voice: Pray the psalm slowly; it's about six verses, so read it at half speed, or walk through its pictures in your mind: a pasture, still water, a dark valley, a table, oil, a full cup, a house. Stop at the picture that fits your life right now: are you at the water, or in the valley? If you pray, say to God there, thou art with me; if you don't, just notice where you are.
Shepherd. The Hebrew word behind the Douay's ruleth me, someone who knows the way leads me, even through the valley. Today's word.
Your line: I shall want nothing. The shepherd knows the way. That's day one hundred sixty-three.

164.title: Lift up your gates (Psalm 23 [24])
164.hook: the earth is the Lord's, and the king of glory comes in
164.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 23 [24] in the Liturgy of the Hours, sometimes as the opening Invitatory psalm, and hear it at Mass in Advent and on feasts like the Presentation of the Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherd, who leads through the valley, not around it. Your line was I shall want nothing. Today, a psalm with a procession in it.

A crowd climbs a hill toward a walled city, singing. At the front, carried on poles, is the ark, the gold-covered chest that, in Israel's scriptures, marks the presence of the invisible God. The city gates are shut. The crowd calls up to them, the watchmen on the walls call back a question, and the crowd answers. Call and response, like a stadium chant. Psalm 23 in the Douay, 24 in most Bibles, may well be the script for that moment.
screen: `A CROWD CLIMBING A HILL.` → `THE ARK AT THE FRONT.` → `THE GATES ARE SHUT.`

segments.voice: It opens wide: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." The ground, the sea, every person on it. Saint Paul quotes this line to settle an argument about food: eat what's sold in the market, he says, because the earth is the Lord's. Then the question at the foot of the hill: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord: or who shall stand in his holy place?" The answer isn't a bloodline or a title: "The innocent in hands, and clean of heart." Clean hands, meaning what you do. A clean heart, meaning what you want. Then the gates: "Lift up your gates, O ye princes, and be ye lifted up, O eternal gates: and the King of Glory shall enter in." From the wall, the challenge: "Who is this King of Glory?" And the crowd: the Lord who is strong and mighty. It happens twice, a chant that builds. Christian readers have heard Christ here: some heard his entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, some the Ascension, heaven's gates opening. An old Christian story tells of Christ going down to the dead on Holy Saturday, and the gates of the underworld hearing this very psalm before they break. And in the older Roman rite of Palm Sunday, the procession stopped outside the shut church door, someone knocked with the foot of the cross, and the gates were sung open.
screen: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `CLEAN HANDS, CLEAN HEART.` · `WHO IS THIS KING OF GLORY?` · `THE DOOR KNOCKED WITH A CROSS.`

segments.voice: Open a window or a door slowly, on purpose, and stand there breathing the outside air; if you can't reach one, picture a door in your home opening wide. Think of the psalm's first line: the street, the neighbors, the weather, all of it the Lord's. If you pray, say lift up your gates, and let God in; if you don't, let the open door be a way of welcoming the day.
Attollite portas. Latin for lift up your gates, the psalm's cry at the city wall, so the King of Glory can come in. Today's word.
Your line: the earth is the lord's. Every bit of it, even the ordinary streets. Until tomorrow.

165.title: The Lord is my light (Psalm 26 [27])
165.hook: whom shall I fear, and one thing I ask, to dwell in his house
165.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 26 [27] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it often at Mass and at funerals, where its line 'one thing I have asked' is often chosen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, attollite portas, a crowd singing at a shut city wall. Your line was the earth is the lord's. Today, a psalm for when you're afraid.

A kid in a dark bedroom. The door is half open. The coat on the chair has become a person. Every sound in the house is a footstep. Then someone flips on the hall light, and the coat is just a coat. Nothing in the room changed. Only the light did. Adults have their own dark rooms: the test results, the layoff rumor, the phone that rings at two in the morning. Psalm 26 in the Douay, 27 in most Bibles, walks straight into that room and turns on the light.
screen: `A COAT BECOMES A PERSON.` → `SOMEONE TURNS ON THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: It opens with a question that's almost a dare: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?" It doesn't say there's nothing out there. The next lines are full of enemies, armies camped around, war rising up. The light doesn't make the danger vanish. It shows who's with you in it. Then the heart of the psalm, a single wish: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life." Out of everything a frightened person might ask for, safety, victory, money, it asks for one thing: to be near God, at home. And it doesn't stay brave the whole way. Halfway through, the voice cracks: don't hide your face from me, don't turn away. Then: "For my father and my mother have left me: but the Lord hath taken me up." It ends not with a feeling but with an instruction to itself: "Expect the Lord, do manfully, and let thy heart take courage, and wait thou for the Lord." Courage here isn't the absence of fear. It's waiting anyway. The Latin first words, Dominus illuminatio mea, are the motto of the University of Oxford, printed on its open book. Jews pray it too: by custom, it's said daily through the season of the High Holy Days.
screen: `WHOM SHALL I FEAR?` · `ONE THING I HAVE ASKED.` · `FATHER AND MOTHER HAVE LEFT ME.` · `WAIT, AND TAKE COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Find the fear sitting closest to you today, the one that turns coats into people, name it plainly in a few words, and picture setting it on the floor beside you like a heavy bag: still there, just not in your hands for now. If you pray, say: the Lord is my light, whom shall I fear? If you don't, simply breathe beside it.
Ori. Hebrew for my light, the psalm's second word, the danger is still there, but the light shows who is with you. Today's word.
Your line: whom shall I fear. It asks it even with enemies all around. Another day on the hill.

166.title: Into thy hands (Psalm 30 [31])
166.hook: the line Jesus prayed as he died, prayed each night at Compline
166.tomorrow: Blessed are they whose sins are covered (Psalm 31 [32])
166.howItsDone: Catholics who pray Night Prayer (Compline) say the short responsory 'Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit' every night; many also pray the line at a deathbed and teach it to children at bedtime.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ori, my light, a psalm that turns on the lamp in a dark room. Your line was whom shall I fear. Today, a line for letting go.

A child at bedtime, in a house where someone prays, says a small memorized line, half asleep. A dying man in a hospital bed says a few last words. Sometimes they're the same kind of line. One sentence in scripture has been said at both moments, by children in bunk beds and monks in choir, by martyrs and, Luke's Gospel says, by Jesus himself. It's only a few words long, and it comes from Psalm 30 in the Douay, 31 in most Bibles.
screen: `THE LAST WORDS AT BEDTIME.` → `THE LAST WORDS AT DEATH.` → `THE SAME LINE.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Into thy hands I commend my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord, the God of truth." Commend means to hand over, to entrust, the way you'd hand someone your child or your keys. The rest of the psalm is someone in real trouble: a net laid for their feet, friends who've turned away, a body worn out with grief. In the middle of it, this one line of handing over. Luke's Gospel says that as Jesus died, he cried out with a loud voice: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." He took the psalm's line and added one word at the front: Father. In Luke, those are his last words. Not a scream, a handing over. Then the line kept going. In the Acts of the Apostles, as Stephen, whom tradition calls the first martyr, is being stoned, he prays: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." The same handing over, now addressed to Jesus. Then the Church made it a nightly habit. For centuries at Compline, the prayer before sleep, monks and nuns have sung a short response built on this verse, In manus tuas, Domine: into your hands, Lord. Sleep, in the old way of thinking, is a small rehearsal for death: you close your eyes and hand yourself over, not knowing for certain you'll wake. So every night becomes practice for letting go. Jews have a neighboring line: the hymn Adon Olam, sung at bedtime and in the synagogue, ends by entrusting the spirit into God's hand.
screen: `COMMEND: TO HAND OVER.` · `FATHER, INTO THY HANDS.` · `STEPHEN: RECEIVE MY SPIRIT.` · `EVERY NIGHT AT COMPLINE.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and think of what you're carrying from today: the undone task, the worry, the person you're anxious about. One by one, picture setting each of them in open hands that aren't yours. If you pray, say the line, into thy hands I commend my spirit; if you don't, simply open your hands and let the day go.
Commend. To hand over, to entrust, the word at the heart of the psalm's line of handing over, prayed by Jesus as he died and by the Church every night. Today's word.
Your line: a small rehearsal for death. Said softly, it's a bedtime prayer. Rest easy.

167.title: Blessed are they whose sins are covered (Psalm 31 [32])
167.hook: one of seven penitential psalms; silence made the bones grow old
167.howItsDone: Catholics have long prayed the seven penitential psalms together, especially during Lent and as preparation for confession; Psalm 31 [32] is also read at Mass and in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, commend, a line of handing over prayed every night at Compline. Your line was a small rehearsal for death. Today, what happens when you don't hand something over.

A dent in someone's car, backed into in a parking lot, and nobody saw. A small lie to a friend. Something broken, said or taken, and never mentioned. At first it's fine. Then it isn't. It sits in the stomach. Whoever is carrying it gets short with people for no reason, avoids a certain face in the hallway, sleeps badly. Nothing outside has changed, but the weight grows. A psalm describes that weight, and what lifted it.
screen: `NOBODY SAW.` → `IT SITS IN THE STOMACH.` → `IT GETS HEAVIER.`

segments.voice: Psalm 31 in the Douay, 32 in most Bibles, starts at the end of the story, with the relief: "Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." Then it goes back to tell how it got there. "Because I was silent my bones grew old; whilst I cried out all the day long." Silent about the sin, groaning about everything else. Day and night, it says, thy hand was heavy upon me. The Hebrew adds that the speaker's strength dried up as in summer heat. That's what the silence cost. Then the turn: "I said I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord: and thou hast forgiven the wickedness of my sin." How fast it happens: I said I will, and it's done. The heaviness was never in the confessing. It was in the not confessing. This is one of seven psalms the Church has long grouped as the penitential psalms, psalms of sorrow for sin; in the Douay they're 6, 31, 37, 50, 101, 129 and 142. Cassiodorus, a sixth-century scholar, wrote about them as a set, and they became a standard devotion in Lent and in old prayer books. Augustine's friend and biographer, Possidius, wrote that as Augustine lay dying, he had these psalms copied and put up on the wall by his bed, and read them, weeping. Saint Paul quotes the opening lines too, to say forgiveness is a gift. Catholic readers often hear in it the logic of confession: say it out loud, and the weight lifts.
screen: `BLESSED ARE THEY WHOSE SINS ARE COVERED.` · `SILENT, MY BONES GREW OLD.` · `I SAID I WILL CONFESS.` · `SEVEN PSALMS OF SORROW.`

segments.voice: Find one small, recent wrong, not the biggest thing in your life: a sharp word, a shortcut, a bit of unkindness, and feel how much it weighs. If you pray, say it plainly to God in a sentence, the way the psalm does: I did this. If you don't, say it plainly to yourself, without excuses, and notice honestly whether anything got lighter.
Penitential psalms. Seven psalms of sorrow for sin that the Church has prayed together for centuries, this one among them. Today's word.
Your line: silence was heavier. The psalm opens with the relief, not the weight. One hundred sixty-seven days, and counting.

168.title: Taste and see (Psalm 33 [34])
168.hook: O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet
168.howItsDone: Catholics hear Psalm 33 [34] at Mass and pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours; its line 'taste and see' has long been sung as a Communion chant and is still used as one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the penitential psalms, and bones grown old from keeping quiet. Your line was silence was heavier. Today closes the week, with a psalm you can taste.

Try describing a ripe peach to someone who has never eaten one. Sweet. Soft. A bit like an apricot. They nod, and still don't know. Then you hand them one, they bite, juice runs down their chin, and now they know, though they couldn't tell you how. Some things you can only learn with your mouth. When the psalmist wanted to say who God is, he didn't reach for an argument. He reached for a kitchen word.
screen: `DESCRIBE A PEACH.` → `THEY STILL DON'T KNOW.` → `THEN THEY TAKE A BITE.`

segments.voice: Psalm 33 in the Douay, 34 in most Bibles. Its heading ties it to a low moment in David's life, when he pretended to be mad to escape a foreign king. Out of that close call comes a song of thanks: "I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth." In Hebrew it's an acrostic: the verses begin, nearly in order, with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, first to last, a way of saying praise from beginning to end. Then the line at its center: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet: blessed is the man that hopeth in him." Taste comes before see. First you try it; then you understand. The psalm isn't asking anyone to agree to an idea about God. It's inviting them to try. Later: "The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a contrite heart: and he will save the humble of spirit." Near to the broken, not the impressive. Christians made it a Communion song. In Jerusalem, in teachings for the newly baptized that tradition credits to Bishop Cyril, the new Christians are told that as they come forward to receive, they will hear a singer chanting, O taste and see. It's still used as a Communion chant today. This week began with a cry from the cross, walked through the shepherd's valley, lifted city gates, turned on a light, handed a spirit over and broke a long silence. It ends here, at a table: taste.
screen: `A SONG AFTER A CLOSE CALL.` · `AN ALPHABET OF PRAISE.` · `TASTE FIRST, THEN SEE.` · `A COMMUNION SONG.`

segments.voice: Take one small bite of something nearby, a piece of fruit, a cracker, a sip of tea, or save this for your next meal; don't chew right away, notice the taste arriving, then chew slowly and notice it change. Don't describe it, just taste. If you pray, give thanks in the psalm's words, taste, and see that the Lord is sweet; if you don't, let the thanks be for the food, and whoever grew it.
Acrostic. A psalm whose verses run through the Hebrew alphabet in order, praise from beginning to end. This one invites you to know God the way you know sweetness: by trying it. Today's word.
Your line: near to the broken. Seven days, seven psalms. That's the week.

fork.setup: someone asks you how to know whether the Lord is good. what does the psalm suggest?
options: wait for a sign in the sky.
fork.reveal: O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet. the psalm invites a trial, not an argument, and early Christians sang it as they came to Communion.

original.note: Hebrew: taste and see, the psalm's invitation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about God being good.
what it means: an invitation to know God by trying, the way you know sweetness, taste first and then see.
what a scholar hears: an alphabet acrostic in Hebrew, and in old Jerusalem teaching, the chant sung as people came to Communion.
